newsitem.title: USA: CBOT wheat sets highs on myriad weather woes.
newsitem.headline: CBOT wheat sets highs on myriad weather woes.

text.p: Myriad weather problems around the world boosted CBOT soft red winter wheat futures to new contract highs in the deferred months, an eight-month high in the May and new crop July was closing in on its one-year high by midsession, traders said.

"Flooding in the northern Plains is very bad and there was very little relief in Europe over the weekend," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter. "There was a little rain in southern France but not much and the forecasts are dry."
Nearby May rallied to a session high of $4.49 per bushel as of 1130 CDT, a fresh eight-month high.

The $4.49 level was last reached by the May on August 13. The active new crop July contract was closing in on its one year high and had traded at $4.59 per bushel as of midsession. July last saw that level on May 2, 1996, reached $4.60 on April 15, 1996 and the contract high for July of $4.65 was set on April 11, 1996.
September set a contract high of $4.63, well above the previous high of $4.50 set Friday.
At 1042 CDT, wheat was two to 10 cents per bushel higher, with May up eight cents at $4.45 a bushel. July was up 9-1/2 at $4.54 and September was up 11 cents at $4.59.

The market was focused on flooding in the northern U.S. spring wheat region, varying opinions about the extent of freeze damage a week ago in U.S. Great Plains hard red winter wheat and on escalating concerns about dry weather in European wheat growing areas.

North Dakota Democratic Congressman Earl Pomeroy Sunday said about 1.7 million acres of North Dakota cropland were under water from the melting of the heavier-than-usual snowfall there and much of that acreage will not go into agricultural production this growing season. North Dakota, especially the Red River Valley region separating North Dakota and Minnesota, is a key U.S. spring wheat growing area.
At 1109 CDT, MGE spring wheat was 8-1/4 cents to 10-1/4 cents per bushel higher and new contract highs had been set in the new crop September contract and in the December contract.

Concern about dry weather in European wheat areas extended from France, the key high quality milling wheat producer into the mainly-feed-wheat-producing area of England. Dry weather in Spain also was cited.
Early wheat was turning yellow in dry eastern England fields and Europeans were puzzling about the crop after a dry spring in the West and bitter cold in the East, sources said.
"Crops are starting to yellow, especially the late drilled ones," one co-op manager in the East England area said. "With no prospect of rain, people are getting concerned."

The impact of the dry weather was most directly felt by farmers who report real signs of damage to cereals in Britain and Spain, European trade sources said. French weather forecasters, officials and farmers have so far refused to talk of a full blown drought, despite irrigation bans in some areas after the prolonged dry spell.
Also, there still hasn't been a definitive statement about the extent of freeze damage that occurred in the U.S. Great Plains hard red winter wheat growing region just over a week ago.
Crop specialists have said the freeze may have sliced more than 100 million bushels from the Kansas wheat crop and severe losses in Oklahoma also were likely.
The market also took note of potential cold weather in Kansas again late this week and China was mentioned as another potential troublesome spot.
"There's talk of a freeze in China and maybe another chance for a freeze in the U.S. late this week," a trader said.
